newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - US debt volatilities rise as bonds slip.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - US debt volatilities rise as bonds slip.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. fixed income options ended higher as underlying markets slid late in the afternoon, dealers said.

Volatilities were initially buoyed by caution ahead of the Treasury's $12.5 billion five-year note auction, traders said. They held on to those early gains as the late selloff kept the market wary of shorting options, they said.

"There was buying coming in in June all day in 10-years and bonds," said a bank affiliate trader at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT). "They started buying during the day, and even after the auction there was still some good buying coming in."
Implied volatility for June T-bond futures options was up 0.4 point to about 10.5 percent, while March rose 0.3 to 10.2.
Early in the session, there was a lot of buying in 10-year note puts with strikes of 107 to 109, traders said. Activity in the five-year area was cautious on moderate volume.
The Treasury's five-year note auction produced a high yield of 6.325 percent and a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.42 times.

Traders said the results were largely in line with their expectations but that the market's reaction, which looked like a repetition of Wednesday's reaction to a two-year note auction, reflected underlying bearishness.
The bond market traded narrowly mixed for some time after the auction results were released in mid-afternoon on both days, but bidders eventually gave in toward the close.

With sentiment tilting toward the bearish side, implied volatilities were likely to be supported on dips for a while, particularly as the release of January employment report due early next month approached, traders said.
They noted that volatilities under 10 percent for a front month option just before a monthly jobs report would be relatively cheap from a historical perspective.
At the shorter end of the yield curve, implied volatilities for Eurodollar options on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange were firmer.
Volatility for June futures options rose 0.1 point to about 12.1 percent, while September was up 0.4 to 15.2.
A CME trader with a bank affiliate said September was gaining more than June probably because of perceived timing of a Federal Reserve move on interest rates.
"There is concern that over the longer term the market will start to move lower," he said. "But in the near term, people are pretty much saying that we're on hold for now.
"For some reason, there doesn't seem to be much fear about the upcoming numbers," he added, referring to a lack of demand for shorter-dated options.

Shorter-dated options, which have higher gamma values and are more sensitive to swings in the underlying market, are typically well bid in an event-driven market, such as just before important economic figures or after a large move in the underlying asset price.
